content: Atopic dermatitis (AD), also known as atopic eczema, is a chronic inflammatory skin condition that significantly impacts the quality of life for both children and adults. The first-line treatment for AD is typically topical corticosteroids (TCS), but their long-term use can lead to notable adverse effects. Tacrolimus ointment, available in two strengths (0.1% and 0.03%), is a potential alternative treatment. Tacrolimus, along with pimecrolimus, belongs to a class of drugs known as topical calcineurin inhibitors (TCIs). The objective of this review was to evaluate the efficacy and safety of topical tacrolimus for moderate to severe atopic dermatitis in comparison to other active treatments. A comprehensive search of multiple databases and trial registries was conducted, and additional data were sought from experts and regulatory bodies. Randomized controlled trials (RCTs) involving children and adults with moderate to severe AD treated with topical tacrolimus were included. The primary outcomes assessed were physician's evaluation, participant's self-assessment of improvement, and adverse effects. Secondary outcomes included validated measures such as SCORAD (SCORing Atopic Dermatitis), EASI (Eczema Area and Severity Index), and BSA (Body Surface Area) scores. A total of 20 studies involving 5,885 participants were included. The variability in drug doses, outcomes, and follow-up periods made meta-analyses challenging. One study demonstrated that tacrolimus 0.1% was superior to low-potency TCS based on physician's assessment (risk ratio [RR] 3.09, 95% confidence interval [CI] 2.14 to 4.45, moderate-quality evidence). Tacrolimus 0.1% also showed marginal superiority over low-potency TCS for the face and neck and moderate-potency TCS for the trunk and extremities (RR 1.32, 95% CI 1.17 to 1.49, moderate-quality evidence). When compared to pimecrolimus 1%, tacrolimus 0.1% nearly doubled the likelihood of improvement as assessed by physicians (RR 1.80, 95% CI 1.34 to 2.42, moderate-quality evidence). The higher concentration of tacrolimus (0.1%) reduced the risk of no improvement by 18% compared to the 0.03% formulation, as evaluated by physicians (RR 0.82, 95% CI 0.72 to 0.92, high-quality evidence). However, when compared to moderate-to-potent TCS, tacrolimus 0.1% showed no significant difference in physician-assessed outcomes, although a marginal benefit was noted in participant-assessed outcomes (RR 1.21, 95% CI 1.13 to 1.29, low-quality evidence) and SCORAD scores. Tacrolimus 0.03% was found to be superior to mild TCS in physician-assessed outcomes (RR 2.58, 95% CI 1.96 to 3.38, moderate-quality evidence) and participant-assessed outcomes (RR 1.64, 95% CI 1.41 to 1.90, moderate-quality evidence). A single trial indicated a moderate benefit of tacrolimus 0.03% over pimecrolimus 1% in physician-assessed outcomes (RR 1.42, 95% CI 1.02 to 1.98, low-quality evidence), but results were inconclusive for BSA scores. When compared to moderate-to-potent TCS, tacrolimus 0.03% showed no significant differences in most outcomes, although a slight advantage for TCS was observed in EASI and BSA scores in two studies. Burning sensations were more frequently reported with calcineurin inhibitors, including tacrolimus 0.03%, compared to corticosteroids (RR 2.48, 95% CI 1.96 to 3.14, high-quality evidence). However, no differences were observed in the incidence of skin infections. These symptoms were generally mild and transient. The overall incidence of adverse events was similar between tacrolimus and pimecrolimus, with minor differences in local effects. Serious adverse events were rare and typically unrelated to treatment. No cases of lymphoma were reported in the included studies or in non-comparative studies, although cases were noted in spontaneous reports, cohorts, and case-control studies. Systemic absorption of tacrolimus was minimal and decreased over time, except in conditions with severe skin barrier defects, such as Netherton's syndrome and lamellar ichthyosis, where higher absorption was reported in case studies. There was no evidence to suggest that topical tacrolimus causes skin atrophy, based on clinical trials, case reports, and in vivo, in vitro, and animal studies. In conclusion, tacrolimus 0.1% was more effective than low-potency corticosteroids, pimecrolimus 1%, and tacrolimus 0.03%. Tacrolimus 0.03% was superior to mild corticosteroids and pimecrolimus. Both formulations of tacrolimus appeared to be safe, with no evidence of increased risk for malignancies or skin atrophy. However, the reliability of the evidence was limited by the lack of data, and the findings should be interpreted with caution. Cost considerations were not evaluated in this review.
